top_choice_rationale: The optical lattice clock (Katori, Ye) is a definite invention whose central claim is complete, reproduced across laboratories and auditable through systematic-uncertainty budgets, with a clean two-name allocation and a citation that can be limited to the invention and its realisation at the 10^-18 level. It is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes. Magic-angle graphene (P001) may be the larger new regime of matter and I rank it second, but its credit set omits key experimentalists such as Cao and Fatemi and the pairing mechanism is still open, so I rate it less secure than P002 today. A prize is preferable to no award, since both proposals describe a discovery or invention of lasting importance.
recusal_note: No direct conflict apparent from profile; Johansson is a Chalmers colleague (not a proponent of P002), and Olsson has long-standing academic exchanges with Japanese universities including a University of Tokyo fellowship, which could be a loose link to Katori's home country, but no documented personal or collaborative tie to any laureate in P001 or P002.
